item.content:encoded:
Pakistan fails to protect children as online sexual abuse cases remain underreported, warns HRCP The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) has raised concerns over the growing threat of online sexual exploitation of children, warning that widespread underreporting, poor coordination among institutions and inadequate protective measures continue to hinder efforts to tackle the problem, as reported by The Express Tribune. ANI | Updated: 28-10-2026 13:27 IST | Created: 28-10-2026 13:27 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) has raised concerns over the growing threat of online sexual exploitation of children, warning that widespread underreporting, poor coordination among institutions and inadequate protective measures continue to hinder efforts to tackle the problem, as reported by The Express Tribune. According to The Express Tribune, in a report, HRCP said online child sexual abuse should not be viewed solely as a cybercrime issue but as a serious violation of children's fundamental rights, dignity and personal safety. Highlighting the scale of the problem, the report cited a 2025 case in Muzaffargarh, where at least 50 children, including those aged six or younger, were allegedly exploited through an international network. Figures from the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children showed that reports concerning suspected child sexual abuse material linked to Pakistan crossed two million in 2021. The HRCP clarified that these figures reflected reports of suspected online activity and did not represent the number of individual victims. The commission urged authorities to improve coordination between child protection agencies, police, cybercrime investigators, prosecutors and courts to strengthen investigations and ensure perpetrators are held accountable. It also stressed that affected children must have access to legal assistance, psychological counselling and rehabilitation services. According to the HRCP, awareness campaigns alone cannot address the crisis without stronger protection systems, institutional accountability and greater responsibility from digital platforms. The commission called for a comprehensive response that prioritises children's safety while ensuring that existing legal and institutional mechanisms are implemented effectively, as cited by The Express Tribune. The warning comes amid further evidence of the scale of online abuse in Pakistan. A separate report launched in September by the National Commission on the Rights of the Child, in collaboration with UNICEF Pakistan, estimated that approximately 1.5 million Pakistani children aged 12 to 17 who used the internet experienced online sexual exploitation and abuse within a single year, as reported by The Express Tribune. (ANI)

item.title: Attack at Balochistan Nushki Girls’ College leaves 3 injured, raising alarm over campus safety
item.description: Three female students were injured after armed, masked men stormed a girls’ degree college in Nushki district, raising concerns over the security of educational institutions in Balochistan, as ...
item.content:encoded:
Attack at Balochistan Nushki Girls’ College leaves 3 injured, raising alarm over campus safety  Three female students were injured after armed, masked men stormed a girls’ degree college in Nushki district, raising concerns over the security of educational institutions in Balochistan, as reported by The Balochistan Post. ANI | Updated: 28-10-2026 12:33 IST | Created: 28-10-2026 12:33 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Three female students were injured after armed, masked men stormed a girls’ degree college in Nushki district, raising concerns over the security of educational institutions in Balochistan, as reported by The Balochistan Post. According to The Balochistan Post, the college administration said that three gunmen entered the premises, damaged surveillance cameras, vandalised the principal’s office and opened fire on students. The injured, identified as Mehmoona, Maryam and Rukhsana, were taken to Mir Gul Khan Naseer Teaching Hospital. Rukhsana was later referred to Quetta due to the seriousness of her injuries. The attackers’ motive remained unclear. The Baloch Students Action Committee (BSAC) condemned the incident, warning that repeated attacks on educational institutions were creating fear among students and undermining education. Its spokesperson noted that teachers and professors had previously been targeted, with students now facing similar violence. The organisation demanded immediate action, justice for the victims and accountability for those responsible. BSAC chairman Uzair Baloch also denounced the shooting, arguing that educational institutions were being targeted to obstruct education in the region. Journalist Bahot Baloch described the attack as an alleged conspiracy to prevent Baloch women from accessing education. He questioned how the gunmen escaped despite security installations reportedly located near the college. The shooting follows another attack on Ruzhn School in Buleda’s Minaz area, where masked gunmen reportedly fired at surveillance cameras. School authorities said several educational institutions in the region had previously faced similar incidents. In Panjgur in 2014, a religious group reportedly threatened private schools, demanding the removal of female students or closure, as highlighted by The Balochistan Post. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan subsequently documented prolonged school closures and sharply reduced attendance following intimidation. Concerns also persist over the safety of educators. Baloch rights organisations have reported the abductions and killings of several teachers, as reported by The Balochistan Post. (ANI)

item.title: Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for USD 47.3m at New York auction
item.description: A rare Nanotyrannus skeleton, belonging to a smaller relative of the T. rex, has sold for USD 47.3 million at an auction at Sotheby’s in New York following a fierce 12-minute bidding war among six ...
item.content:encoded:
Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for USD 47.3m at New York auction A rare Nanotyrannus skeleton, belonging to a smaller relative of the T. rex, has sold for USD 47.3 million at an auction at Sotheby’s in New York following a fierce 12-minute bidding war among six contenders. ANI | Updated: 28-10-2026 11:54 IST | Created: 28-10-2026 11:54 IST

Nanotyrannus skeleton (Image source: Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

A rare Nanotyrannus skeleton, belonging to a smaller relative of the T. rex, has sold for USD 47.3 million at an auction at Sotheby’s in New York following a fierce 12-minute bidding war among six contenders. The specimen, named Jodi, is one of only three relatively complete Nanotyrannus skeletons known to science. Blowing well past an estimate of USD 6 to USD 9 million, the sale narrowly missed the auction record for a fossil, set in July with the sale of Gus — an exceptional T. rex skeleton that went under the hammer for USD 50.1 million, as per CNN. Standing 9.6 feet tall and measuring 19.6 feet long, Jodi is just over half the length of Gus. The scarcity of comparable specimens is likely to have contributed to the eye-watering sale price. However, the very existence of Nanotyrannus as a distinct species remains hotly debated among paleontologists. Only recently have researchers increasingly come to favor the view that Nanotyrannus was a separate species rather than a juvenile T. rex. The specimen, according to Sotheby’s, is exceptionally preserved, made up of 191 bone elements, and includes a “virtually complete” skull. The skeleton was discovered in 2019 by Montana rancher Jodi Pierson, who inspired its name, and excavated by Clayton Phipps, a commercial paleontologist nicknamed the “Dinosaur Cowboy.” Like several other important fossils previously sold at auction, Jodi comes from Hell Creek Formation, a geological boneyard stretching across Montana, Wyoming and the Dakotas. One of the first skeletons of T. rex was found there in 1902, and the name T. rex was given to the species based on fossils unearthed in the area, according to CNN. Based on the overall size and bone development, Jodi is an adult specimen, according to Sotheby’s. The missing bones have been replaced with custom 3D printed and sculpted elements, and the fossil was offered with “full rights,” meaning it doesn’t contain any copyrighted elements from other dinosaurs. Its new owner — whose identity is unknown — can therefore create replicas of the skeleton and sell them to museums or collectors. (ANI)

item.title: “I ended eight wars": Trump reiterates claim to have ended India-Pak conflict
item.description: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) claimed that he helped end the India-Pakistan conflict by threatening to impose 250 per cent tariffs on both countries, reiterating that he used ...
item.content:encoded:
“I ended eight wars": Trump reiterates claim to have ended India-Pak conflict US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) claimed that he helped end the India-Pakistan conflict by threatening to impose 250 per cent tariffs on both countries, reiterating that he used trade as leverage to prevent further escalation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours. ANI | Updated: 28-10-2026 11:33 IST | Created: 28-10-2026 11:33 IST

US President Donald Trump (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) claimed that he helped end the India-Pakistan conflict by allegedly threatening to impose 250 per cent tariffs on both countries, reiterating that he used trade as leverage to prevent further escalation between the two nuclear-armed neighbours. Addressing supporters at a midterm election rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, Trump said five of the eight wars he claimed to have ended were resolved through trade-related measures, citing India and Pakistan as an example. “I ended eight wars, but five of them were ended by the use of trade, like India and Pakistan,” Trump said. His claim of ending eight wars came against the selection of Indian-origin South African jurist Navi Pillay for the Nobel Peace Prize. During the rally, he called her a "woman that nobody ever heard of." Recalling his intervention during the military confrontation, Trump said he had contacted the prime ministers of India and Pakistan and warned them of severe economic consequences if hostilities continued. “I called up two great prime ministers. I said, ‘Look, here's the story: If you go to war--they already shot down 11 planes, 11 planes, but they were in the midst, they were a week and a half in. Would you agree, Ted, that war was raging? And they're nuclear powers, it would have been terrible,’” Trump said. He added that he threatened to impose steep tariffs on both countries to discourage further fighting. “And I said, if you go to war, if you keep doing this, I'm going to put 250% tariff on each of you, and you're never going to be able to do business in the United States,” Trump said. Recalling the response to his warning, Trump said the leaders initially objected, but he insisted that he would proceed with the proposed tariffs. “‘No, no, no, you can't do--’ I said, ‘I'm going to do it,’” he said. Trump suggested that the tariff threat may have given both sides a reason to step back from further confrontation. “They might have been happy that I did it. Maybe it was an excuse for them not to fight. Who the hell wants to fight like that?” he said. The US President further claimed that hostilities ended immediately after his intervention and cited remarks he attributed to Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. “But they immediately ended the war, and the Prime Minister of Pakistan, highly respected man, said, ‘President Donald Trump saved at least 30 million lives.’ At least,” Trump said. Earlier on October 23, as well, Trump had once again claimed credit for averting a military confrontation between India and Pakistan. Addressing a campaign rally in Florida, boasting of his diplomatic interventions on the international stage, Trump said his direct ultimatum to the leadership of both countries swiftly brought hostilities to an end. "You stop India and Pakistan, two nuclear nations. I said, 'Fellas, if you guys are going to do that, you're not going to trade with the United States. I'm going to put massive tariffs on both of you, 250 per cent, so you won't be able to do any business,” US President said. Claiming that the warning forced both sides to back off, Trump added, “They got very upset, very angry; they stopped shooting, and the war was over. Eleven planes were shot. I stopped all these wars, and it's really an honour to do so." Expressing unfairness over not receiving international accolades for his claimed diplomatic interventions, Trump remarked, "I've settled eight wars. Did I get the Nobel Prize? No." Meanwhile, India has consistently disputed Trump's claims regarding the loss of 11 aircraft during the engagement while remaining steadfast in rejecting any external mediation. India has reiterated that the ceasefire understanding during Operation Sindoor was reached only after Pakistan's Director General of Military Operations (DGMO) reached out to his Indian counterpart to request a halt in military action. India had launched Operation Sindoor on May 7 last year as a decisive, targeted response to destroy terror infrastructure across Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK). The anti-terror operation was carried out to dismantle terror bases that were utilised to plan the horrific April 22 terrorist attack in Pahalgam. Following effective Indian strikes that dismantled key terror launchpads, the operation was paused on May 10 after a formal request from the Pakistani side. On October 10, Trump continued to criticise the decision to award the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Indian-origin South African jurist Navi Pillay, claiming that he had settled eight wars, is close to ending or settling two more conflicts and deserved the prestigious honour for his efforts. In a post on Truth Social, Trump listed his claimed achievements in resolving international conflicts, securing the release of hostages and preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, while questioning why he or the United States did not receive the award. Trump's remarks came after the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced on October 9 that Pillay had been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. (ANI)
